thread.title: Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) the parent company of Google, re

author: Feria Investor
title: Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) the parent company of Google, re
text:
Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ), the parent company of Google, reports Q4 earnings after the close of the market on Thursday. We would like to take a look at what investors expect and address how tax reform could strike the Internet giant like colleagues Apple ( AAPL ) and Facebook ( FB ).
Earnings Expectations Alphabet is expected to have had a strong holiday quarter. Retailers spending on digital advertising typically increase their spend during this time to attract more traffic.
Wall Street expects the company to report a $10.12 EPS and to bring in roughly $25.6bn in revenue. Estimize, the crowd-sourced earnings estimate community, sources hundreds of investors on every stock and often more accurately predicts actual results for companies like Alphabet. Take a look at the revenue estimates:

Actual results (green slope) have eclipsed both Wall Street and Estimize, and expectations of $25.6-25.8bn could be beat again.

We see a similar history for EPS, and notably the last two quarters Alphabet vastly outperformed expectations. As we will detail below, this may be the case again in light of recent tax law changes.
Alphabet's Traffic Acquisition Costs (TACs) and Cost Per Click (CPC) are the data points analysts look at closely to gauge the health of the company's core digital advertising business. Facebook and Google are the behemoths in this industry, receiving upwards of 50% of all ad dollars spent online:

Analysts worry about how much Alphabet must pay, or its Traffic Acquisition Costs, to really attract customers. Though higher TAC may have characterized the last few quarters, trends are now expected to improve for the company. Investors will look closely at these numbers to assess such a trend and to see whether the company is making headway here.
Falling CPC, or Cost Per Click, also may see a trend reversal with this report. Facebook, the main competitor to Alphabet for digital ad dollars, actually reported a rise in the prices it has been able to charge advertisers (some speculating the rise in the stock after hours from previously lower levels was caused by this information). If Alphabet can somehow report impressive numbers here, the stock could perform similarly well.
"Other Bets" segments that include Internet of Things projects like Nest and self-driving endeavors like Waymo also may attract interest, but it is the advertising business that dominates Alphabet's numbers.
Taxes The tax law changes enacted by the US will certainly be a focal point of the report. Alphabet currently holds more than $60 billion of its $100 billion-plus in cash overseas. As the deemed repatriation provision treats overseas cash as if it was already repatriated, Alphabet is set to pay a roughly 15% tax rate to the tune of $10bn. Once this charge is viewed in context, the next question will certainly be what to do with all the money at its disposal.
Share repurchases, always a popular option among these large companies, may certainly be waiting in the wings. Alphabet would be paying a pretty high price, however, as it nears its trillion-dollar market cap and stock prices near all-time highs. Perhaps the beginnings of a dividend?
While the opportunity for a one-time, special dividend keeps management's responsibilities low, it is also not out of the question to consider a quarterly dividend from Alphabet. With around 600mn shares outstanding, the company could easily issue a $10/share special dividend with roughly 10% of its overseas cash. That sounds pretty shareholder friendly. It could alternatively seek out a quarterly dividend as it returns cash more consistently.
Finally, more M&A can await Alphabet - management typically hedges when asked about it however. Often remarks like "we will always look at opportunities" or "taxes don't affect whether we make key investments," etc. So we may not receive much insight in that regard.
Conclusion The latest earnings report should build off the strong holiday quarter and may give us insight into how Alphabet will begin spending its overseas cash.
